problem: The Sharpe ratio is described wrongly. Sharpe divides the average excess return by the SD of returns, that is (mean return − risk-free rate)/SD. The chapter says it divides SD by the average return, which is the inverse of the CV and also drops the risk-free rate.
fix: The same idea appears in finance as the Sharpe ratio, which divides the average excess return (average return minus the risk-free rate) by the SD of returns. Note it is the CV turned upside down: return per unit of risk instead of risk per unit of return.

problem: "A Gini of 0.372 is a proportion, not 37.2%, unless a percentage is asked" reads as if 37.2% were a different quantity. A proportion and its percentage are the same value, so a student may conclude 0.372 must never be written as 37.2%.
fix: A Gini of 0.372 is a pure number between 0 and 1; written as a percentage it is 37.2%. Never write 0.372%, and never attach a unit to it.

problem: The two forms are joined with "=", but (mean − mode)/SD = 3(mean − median)/SD is an empirical relation that holds only for moderately skewed distributions (it comes from mode ≈ mean − 3(mean − median)), not an exact identity for every distribution.
fix: Write Sk = (mean − mode)/SD, and for moderately skewed data use the equivalent form 3(mean − median)/SD, which avoids needing the mode.

problem: The text says G = 1 means one household takes all, but the given grouped formula can never reach 1 with a finite number of groups: with n equal groups its maximum is 1 − 1/n, for example 0.8 with five groups.
fix: Add that G = 1 is the limiting case of infinitely many households; with n equal groups the grouped formula tops out at 1 − 1/n, so the computed Gini is a slight understatement for small n.
